performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: A solo violin ventures onto the ice above a long bass F; before long, everyone is slipping. Vivaldi ends the concerto with the Sirocco and north wind fighting through the strings.

sections.label: A · A violin on the ice
sections.mNote: The solo circles above a long F in the bass

sections.label: B · Cautious steps, then a fall
sections.mNote: The strings join over C and tumble downwards

sections.label: C · Running across the ice
sections.mNote: The solo’s detached semiquavers climb above held strings

sections.label: D · The ice breaks
sections.mNote: Short string phrases break apart in C minor

sections.label: E · The Sirocco without basses
sections.mNote: Lento in E♭ major; the low strings fall silent

sections.label: F · The winds go to war
sections.mNote: Solo runs alternate with repeated-note orchestral gusts

sections.label: F′ · The last F-minor gusts
sections.mNote: The full strings carry the wind figures to the cadence

cues.title: A foot on the ice
cues.text: “Caminar Sopra’l giaccio, e à passo lento / Per timor di cader gersene intenti” — “To walk on ice with slow steps, taking care for fear of falling.” The 1725 sonnet begins cautiously. The solo violin changes direction above a long F; the other upper strings wait.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, letters F–G; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, III, bars 1–20: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351. The sonnets were published anonymously with Op. 8.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Down, then up again
cues.text: “Gir forte Sdruzziolar, cader à terra / Di nuovo ir Sopra ’l giaccio e correr forte” — “Turn sharply, slip, fall to the ground; go back onto the ice and run hard.” After the orchestra’s falling scales, the solo violin scrambles upwards in detached semiquavers.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letters H–I; translation ours. Mutopia score, III, bars 40–60, including Cader à terra at bar 48 and Correr forte at bar 51: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Cracks between the notes
cues.text: “Sin ch’il giaccio Si rompe, e Si disserra” — “Until the ice breaks and splits open.” The strings interrupt their running with short notes and gaps. Little bursts of demisemiquavers fill the cracks before the soloist takes over again.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter L; translation ours. Mutopia score, III, bars 85–100, especially the rests and short figures at bars 89–92: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Beyond the iron gates
cues.text: “Sentir uscir dalle ferrate porte” — “To hear emerging from the iron gates.” The sonnet unleashes the winds. For the Sirocco, Vivaldi writes Lento in E♭ major and removes the bass entirely. Only the upper strings remain.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter M; translation ours. Mutopia score, III, bars 101–119, marked Il Vento Sirocco and Lento, with basso tacet: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The winds at war
cues.text: “Sirocco, Borea, e tutti i Venti in guerra” — “Sirocco, Boreas, and all the winds at war.” Solo runs collide with orchestral bursts. The sonnet ends: “Quest’è ’l verno, mà tal, che gioja apporte” — “This is winter, yet it brings joy.” Vivaldi drives the strings towards F minor.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter N and final line; translation ours. Mutopia score, III, bars 120–153; the last line is printed above the closing bars: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: F moves to C
transitions.from: A · A violin on the ice
transitions.to: B · Cautious steps, then a fall
transitions.how: The bass changes its long F to C, the dominant of F minor. The orchestral strings join the soloist, first in running semiquavers, then in cautious quavers. The C stays underneath as the steps grow more insistent and the falling scales begin.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 21–50; the dominant pedal and walking episode are described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php.

transitions.title: F minor after the fall
transitions.from: B · Cautious steps, then a fall
transitions.how: The strings tumble down in scales, then the soloist starts running from F. Its detached semiquavers climb above held upper-string notes. The basso briefly rests; the solo travels from F minor towards C minor, where long C and G pedals support the later passage.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 48–84; harmonic route at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php.

transitions.title: The C-minor run breaks apart
transitions.how: The solo’s descending triplets reach a tutti in C minor. Running scales break into short notes, rests and little demisemiquaver flurries. G, the dominant, supports the exchanges before the solo finishes the passage on a low G.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 80–100: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351; C-minor context described by Rodríguez Alvira.

transitions.title: The bass vanishes in E♭
transitions.how: The C-minor solo ends on G. At the Lento the upper strings begin in E♭ major, and the basso falls silent for nineteen bars. The violin’s opening G–F–E♭ now moves in quavers under the words Il Vento Sirocco.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 100–119; E♭ major identified at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php.

transitions.title: The north wind starts on E♭
transitions.to: F · The winds go to war
transitions.how: The solo violin bursts into demisemiquavers on E♭, under the words naming Boreas and all the winds. Repeated-note tutti gusts interrupt its runs and bring the bass back. The episode leaves E♭ major and reaches F minor.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, bars 120–139; harmonic route described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/03.php.

transitions.title: The whole orchestra becomes the wind
transitions.from: F · The winds go to war
transitions.how: The soloist rejoins the full strings in F minor. Their repeated demisemiquavers and downward runs extend the wind music through the final tutti. E♮ sharpens the approach to F before the last held chord.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, III, closing tutti, bars 137–153: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: III. Allegro; solo opening, basso pedals, bars 101–119 basso tacet, and final wind episodes. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

timeline.note: The solo violin moves over the long F bass; orchestral upper strings rest.
Upper strings join over the held dominant C.
Running solo over sustained upper-string support; the basso briefly rests.
Low pedal support resumes beneath the continuing solo passage.
Tutti interruptions and a solo link alternate in this region.
The Sirocco Lento removes the basso for nineteen bars.
Rapid solo figures alternate with short orchestral wind bursts; participation is intermittent.
The full-string wind figures drive the conclusion.

composer.epithet: He wrote concertos for the women of Venice’s Pietà, operas for its theatres, and a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 a twenty-five-year-old Venetian became a priest in March and a violin teacher in September. Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and continued helping with his career long after the son had become famous. Venice knew Antonio as il prete rosso, the red priest. His working places would be the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year: in 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 took him back. The music survived the office politics.
